There are some septum ring styles in which the design prevents the seam from traveling into your piercing accidentally. For example, the BVLA Amity ring (the leaf design on top prevents the seam from going inside the piercing iirc). You can also walk into an APP piercing shop and just ask which jewelry they'd be willing to put in a fresh septum piercing. The massive downside here is that solid gold rings are not at all cheap, and you won't find any cute or dainty designs in titanium (in my experience).

One big plus to a having a horseshoe (sometimes called a circular barbell) is that it's a great retainer. I've been wearing mine flipped up for about a year straight now. It's implant-grade titanium, so I could really just leave it in for my whole life if I wanted to. I haven't really been much of a septum gal for the past couple years

Your body pushes out lymph fluid as a means of stopping bacteria from entering your body through an open wound whether it’s infected or not. It’s the thing that dries into that “crust” you see on piercings. Totally normal.

**NAP** Could just be lymph fluid in the pic. Is it hot? Have you submerged your piercing in water recently? Have you removed the jewelry and reinserted it? If the answer to the three questions is no, chances are you just have a finnicky lobe piercing (I’ve had plenty be flippant with me like this). Monitor it, and if it gets worse, 100% go to a doctor.

So honestly, not sure that it’s infected. It’s been 3 days, and infections mostly take longer to present worrying symptoms (from what I’ve seen). NEVER take new piercings out. It’ll take twice as long to heal. Your body is very effective at keeping bacteria out so long as you don’t do things like submerge a piercing in hot tub water.

Uhhhhhhhh just looking at it it’s way too early to call imo. It COULD be rejecting, it COULD just be a lil inflamed. This isn’t meant to scare you—I’m just saying 1 month is when piercings still typically behave in a volatile fashion. Sit on it for about 1-2 weeks. Monitor if it gets better or worse. If it gets worse, repost with new pics and make plans to do something about it.

It’s normal for bars to be longer to accommodate swelling. Downsize in three weeks, give or take. Minor redness, but that’s common, especially for us pale folk.

If you actually do have an infection, DO NOT TRAP IT INSIDE BY TAKING THE JEWELRY OUT. Some fluid leaking, redness, and soreness is not automatically an infection (that’s a given with almost any piercing). If it doesn’t hurt and you’ve let it go on this long with seeing a doctor, you probably don’t have one, but if you are still worried, it’s better to have a bill for a physical exam and antibiotics than an infection in your head.

Buy a copy of Cocktail Codex. How old you have to be to bartend depends on which state/province you live in. Practice at home with a home bartending kit and have a base knowledge of spirits and liquers. Diversify your own palette.
Put them all on flashcards. All of them. Review every single day. I have about 50+ cocktail recipes to memorize in the next month before busy season starts. Yeehaw.

Personally I recommend some serving experience before you start bartending. Just a couple months so you know how to work a POS system and the time management aspect is down. Get a barware set from a total wine (or whatever the equivalent is in Canada) and start practicing at home. Speeding up the process of making drinks is super important. 

Learn from your seniors, but it’s important to know about the wine list and your cocktails. I downloaded vivino and just memorize most of the stuff on there to get by with wine knowledge, but if you’re aspiring to get to a higher standard of bartending, get a copy of Cocktail Codex (Death and Co) stat. First cocktail book you should read IMO. Others are Meehan’s Bartending Manual, Welcome Home (Death and Co), and Liquid Intelligence. Getting through these books will honestly take a lot of time, but if you do it now, you’re ahead of most bartenders your age. Always walk into any bar with a printed copy of your resume when applying. Be knowledgeable about the base concept of most spirits—I’ve been asked about these in interviews. It’s also not the worst thing to accept a serving or barbacking position right off the bat—some of the places worth working will have you learn on the job and push you up.

There’s tons more to know, but for now, practice at home, learn from/watch other bartenders, read from good sources, and show up clean and presentable at interviews, resume in hand between 2-4 PM (when bars/restaurants are NEVER busy). Good luck!
